source_text: Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo ait: etsi ego de me testificor, uerum est testimonium meum, quia scio unde uenerim et guo eam, uos ignoratis unde uenerim aut quo eam, uos secundum carnem iudicatis? ecce et hic illuc se dicit rediturum, unde se testificatur ante uenisse, missum scilicet de caelo. descendit ergo unde uenit, quo modo illuc uadit unde descendit. ex quo, si homo tantummodo Christus esset, non inde uenisset: atque ideo nec illuc abiret, quoniam non inde uenisset. ueniendo autem inde, unde homo uenire non potest, deum se ostendit uenisse. sed enim huius ipsius descensionis ignari et imperiti Iudaei heredes sibi haereticos istos reddiderunt, quibus dicitur: vos ignoratis unde ueniam, et quo eam: uos secundum carnem tudicatis. tam isti quam Iudaei, carnalem solam esse Christi natiuitatem tenentes, nihil aliud Christum esse quam hominem crediderunt, non considerantes illud, quoniam, cum de caelo homo non potuerit uenire, ut merito illuc posset redire, deum esse qui inde descenderit, unde homo uenire non potuerit. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo dicit: vos ex inferioribus estis, ego desursum sum; uos de hoc mundo estis, ego non sum de hoc mundo? ideo autem si omnis homo ex hoc mundo est, et ideo in hoc mundo est Christus, an homo tantummodo est? absit. sed considera quod ait: ego non sum de hoc mundo. numquid ergo mentitur, cum ex hoc mundo sit, si homo tantummodo sit? aut si non mentitur, non est ex hoc mundo. non ergo homo tantummodo est, quia ex hoc mundo non est. sed ne lateret quis esset, expressit unde esset: ego, inquit, desursum sum; hoc est, de caelo, unde homo uenire non potest; non enim in caelo factus est. deus est ergo qui desursum est, et idcirco de hoc mundo non est. quamquam etiam quodam modo ex hoc mundo est; unde non deus tantum est Christus, sed et homo; ut merito, quo modo non est ex hoc mundo secundum uerbi diuinitatem, ita ex hoc mundo sit secundum suscepti corporis fragilitatem. homo est enim cum deo iunctus, et deus cum homine copulatus. sed idcirco nunc hic Christus in unam partem solius diuinitatis incubuit, quoniam caecitas Iudaica solam in Christo partem carnis aspexit, et inde in praesenti loco, silentio praeterita corporis fragilitate quae de mundo est, de sua sola diuinitate locutus est, quae de mundo non est: ut in quantum illi inclinauerant, ut hominem illum tantummodo crederent, in tantum illos Christus posset ad diuinitatem suam considerandam trahere, ut re deum crederent, uolens illorum incredulitatem circa diuinitatem suam, omissa interim commemoratione sortis humanae, solius diuinitatis oppositione superare. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo dicit: ego ex deo prodii et ueni, cum constet hominem a deo factum esse, non ex deo processisse? ex deo autem homo quo modo non processit, sic dei uerbum processit; de quo dictum est: eructauit cor meum uerbum bonum. quod quoniam ex deo est, merito et apud deum est: quodque, quia non otiose prolatum est, merito omnia facit; omnia enim per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil. sed enim hoc uerbum, per quod facta sunt omnia, deo, dum qui processit sermo, deus est qui processit ex deo. si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo ait: sz gués uerbum meum Seruauerit, mortem non uidebit in aeternum? mortem in aeternum non uidere, quid aliud quam immortalitas est? immortalitas autem diuinitati socia est, quia et diuinitas immortalis est, et immortalitas diuinitatis fructus est. sed enim omnis homo mortalis est; immortalitas autem ex mortali non potest esse. ergo ex Christo homine mortali immortalitas non potest nasci. sed qui uerbum custodierit, inquit, meum, mortem non uidebit in aeternum. ergo uerbum Christi praestat immortalitatem, et per immortalitatem praestat diuinitatem. quod si non potest exhibere ut immortalem alterum faciat ipse mortalis, hoc autem Christi uerbum exhibet pariter et praestat immortalitatem, non utique homo tantum est, qui praestat immortalitatem, quam, si tantummodo homo esset, praestare non posset. praestando autem diuinitatem per immortalitatem, deum se probat diuinitatem porrigendo, quam, nisi deus esset, praestare non posset. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo inquit: ante Abraham ego sum? nemo enim hominum ante eum potest esse ex quo ipse est; nec potest fieri ut quicquam prius fuerit ante illum ex quo ipsum originem sumpsit. sed enim Christus, cum ex Abraham sit, ante Abraham esse se dicit. aut mentitur et fallit, si ante Abraham non fuit, qui ex Abraham fuit: aut non fallit, si etiam deus est, dum ante Abraham fuit. quod nisi fuisset, consequenter, cum ex Abraham fuisset, ante Abraham esse non posset. si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo ait: ef ego agnoscam eas et sequuntur me meae; et ego uitam aeternam do illis, et numquam peribunt in perpetuum? sed enim cum omnis homo mortalitatis ro sit legibus alligatus, et idcirco in perpetuum se ipse seruare non possit, multo magis in perpetuum alterum seruare non poterit. at in perpetuum se Christus repromittit salutem daturum; quam si non dat, mendax est: si dat, deus est. sed non fallit; dat enim quod repromittit. deus est ergo, qui salutem perpetuam porrigit; quam homo, qui se ipsum seruare non potest, alteri praestare non poterit. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quid est, quod ait: ego e pater unum sumus? quomodo enim ego et pater unum sumus, Si non et deus est et filius? qui idcirco unum potest dici, dum ex ipso est, et dum filius eius est, et dum ex ipso nascitur, dum ex ipso processisse reperitur; per quod et deus est. quod cum inuidiosum Iudaei putassent, et blasphemum credidissent, eo quod se ostenderat his sermonibus Christus esse deum, ac propterea ad lapides concurrissent, et saxorum ictus inicere gestissent, exemplo et testimonio scripturarum aduersarios suos fortiter refutauit. sz zos, inquit, dixit deos ad quos det uerba facta sunt, et non potest solui scriptura; quem pater sanctificauit et misit in hunc mundum uos dicitis, quia blasphemas, quia dixi: filius dei sum ego? quibus uocibus neque se negauit deum, quin immo deum se esse firmauit. nam quia sine dubitatione dii esse dicuntur, ad quos uerba dei facta sunt, multo magis hic deus, qui melior illis omnibus inuenitur. et nihilominus calumniosam blasphemiam dispositione legitima congruenter refutauit: deum enim se sic intellegi uult, ut filium dei et non ipsum patrem uellet intellegi. missum enim se esse dixit, et multa opera se ex patre ostendisse monstrauit; ex quo non patrem se sed filium esse intellegi uoluit; ultima parte defensionis filii, non patris, fecit mentionem SUM. ita quod ad crimen blasphemiae pertinet, filium se non patrem dicit: quod autem ad diuinitatem spectet ipsius, ego e pater unum sumus dicendo, filium se esse et deum probauit. deus est ergo: deus autem sic, ut filius sit, non pater.
pass_a_gloss: If Christ is only a man, how does he say: even if I testify about myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going, but you do not know where I came from or where I am going, you judge according to the flesh? Behold, he also says here that he is going back to where he came from, whence he testifies that he came before, namely, having been sent from heaven. Therefore, he descends from where he came, just as he goes to where he descended. From this, if Christ were only a man, he would not have come from there: and therefore, he would not go away from there either, because he did not come from there. But by coming from where a man cannot come, he shows that he came as God. The Jews, however, who are ignorant and unskilled in this very descent, have handed down to these heretics, who are told: you do not know where I come from and where I am going, you judge according to the flesh. Both these heretics and the Jews, holding that Christ's birth is only fleshly, have believed that Christ is nothing but a man, not considering that, since a man cannot come from heaven, so that he might rightly return there, he who descended from where a man cannot come is God. If Christ is only a man, how does he say: you are from below, I am from above; you are of this world, I am not of this world? For if every man is of this world and therefore Christ is in this world, is he only a man? Absolutely not. But consider what he says: I am not of this world. Is he lying when he is of this world, if he is only a man? Or if he is not lying, he is not of this world. Therefore, he is not only a man, because he is not of this world. But lest anyone be unaware of who he is, he expressed where he is from: I, he says, am from above; that is, from heaven, where a man cannot come; for he was not made in heaven. Therefore, he who is from above is God, and for this reason, he is not of this world. Although he is also in a certain way of this world; whence Christ is not only God but also a man; so that rightly, just as he is not of this world according to the divinity of the Word, so he is of this world according to the frailty of the assumed body. For a man is joined with God, and God is coupled with a man. But for now, Christ has inclined to the part of his divinity alone, because Jewish blindness has seen only the part of the flesh in Christ, and from this present place, passing over in silence the frailty of the body which is of the world, he has spoken of his divinity alone, which is not of the world: so that inasmuch as they have inclined to believe that he is only a man, Christ can draw them to consider his divinity, so that they may believe him to be God, willing to overcome their unbelief about his divinity, omitting for the time being the mention of his human lot, by the opposition of his divinity alone. If Christ is only a man, how does he say: I came forth from God and came, when it is clear that man was made by God, not proceeding from God? But just as man did not proceed from God, so the Word of God proceeded; of which it is said: my heart has uttered a good word. Which, since it is from God, is rightly also with God: and since it was not uttered idly, it rightly does all things; for all things were made through it, and without it, nothing was made. But this Word, through which all things were made, is God, since the one who proceeded is the Word, and God is the one who proceeded from God. If Christ is only a man, how does he say: he who keeps my word will not see death in eternity? Not seeing death in eternity is nothing other than immortality. And immortality is a companion of divinity, because divinity is immortal, and immortality is the fruit of divinity. But every man is mortal; immortality, however, cannot be from what is mortal. Therefore, immortality cannot arise from Christ as a mortal man. But he who keeps my word, he says, will not see death in eternity. Therefore, Christ's Word provides immortality, and through immortality, it provides divinity. Which, if he cannot exhibit so as to make another immortal, being himself mortal, but Christ's Word exhibits and provides immortality, then he who provides immortality is not only a man, because he provides what, if he were only a man, he could not provide. By providing divinity through immortality, he proves himself to be God, offering divinity, which he could not provide if he were not God. If Christ is only a man, how does he say: before Abraham, I am? For no man can be before Abraham, from whom he himself is; nor can it happen that anything was before him, from whom he himself originated. But Christ, since he is from Abraham, says that he is before Abraham. Either he is lying and deceiving, if he was not before Abraham, who is from Abraham: or he is not deceiving, if he is also God, since he was before Abraham. Which, if he had not been, it would follow that, since he is from Abraham, he could not be before Abraham. If Christ is only a man, how does he say: I will know them and they will follow me, and I will give them eternal life, and they will never perish in eternity? But since every man is bound by the laws of mortality and therefore cannot preserve himself in eternity, much more can he not preserve another in eternity. But Christ promises to give salvation in eternity; which, if he does not give, he is a liar: if he gives, he is God. But he does not lie; for he gives what he promises. Therefore, he is God, who offers eternal salvation; which a man, who cannot preserve himself, cannot provide to another. If Christ is only a man, what is the meaning of his saying: I and the Father are one? For how can it be said that I and the Father are one, if he is not also God and the Son? Who can be said to be one, because he is from the Father, and because he is the Son of the Father, and because he is born of the Father, and because he is found to have proceeded from the Father; through which he is also God. Which, when the Jews considered it to be arrogant and blasphemous, because Christ showed himself to be God in these words, and therefore they rushed to stones and prepared to throw them, Christ strongly refuted his adversaries with the example and testimony of the Scriptures. For he said: has it not been said to those to whom the word of God came, and can the Scripture not be dissolved? Whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, you say that I blaspheme, because I said: I am the Son of God? To which words he did not deny that he is God, but rather confirmed that he is God. For since those to whom the words of God came are called gods, much more is this God, who is found to be better than all of them. And nevertheless, he refuted the calumnious blasphemy with a legitimate disposition: for he wants to be understood as God, so that he is the Son of God, and not the Father himself. For he said that he was sent, and he showed that he had performed many works from the Father; from which he wanted to be understood as the Son, not the Father; he made mention of the Son, not the Father, in the last part of his defense. So, as far as the crime of blasphemy is concerned, he says that he is the Son, not the Father: but as far as his divinity is concerned, by saying I and the Father are one, he proved himself to be the Son and God. Therefore, he is God: but God in such a way that he is the Son, not the Father.

pass_b_english: If Christ is only a man, how can he say, "Even if I testify about myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going, but you do not know where I came from or where I am going"? You judge according to the flesh (John 8:23). Look, he also says here that he is going back to the place from which he came, the place he testifies he came from before, having been sent from heaven. Therefore, he descends from where he came, just as he goes to where he descended. From this it follows that if Christ were only a man, he would not have come from there, and so he would not go back there either, because he did not come from there. But by coming from where a man cannot come, he shows that he came as God.

The Jews, however, who are ignorant and unskilled in this very descent, have handed these heretics down as their heirs, heretics who are told, "You do not know where I come from or where I am going; you judge according to the flesh" (John 8:23). Both these heretics and the Jews, holding that Christ's birth is only fleshly, have believed that Christ is nothing but a man. They do not consider that since a man cannot come from heaven so that he might rightly return there, the one who descended from where a man cannot come is God.

If Christ is only a man, how can he say, "You are from below, I am from above; you are of this world, I am not of this world" (John 8:23)? For if every man is of this world, and therefore Christ is in this world, is he only a man? Absolutely not. Consider what he says: "I am not of this world." Is he lying when he is of this world, if he is only a man? Or if he is not lying, he is not of this world. Therefore, he is not only a man, because he is not of this world. But lest anyone be unaware of who he is, he declared where he is from: "I am from above"—that is, from heaven, where a man cannot come, for he was not made in heaven. Therefore, the one who is from above is God, and for this reason he is not of this world. Although he is also in a certain way of this world; therefore Christ is not only God but also a man, so that just as he is not of this world according to the divinity of the Word, so he is of this world according to the frailty of the assumed body. For a man is joined with God, and God is coupled with a man. But for now Christ has leaned toward the side of his divinity alone, because Jewish blindness saw only the fleshly part in Christ, and from this present place, passing over in silence the frailty of the body which is of the world, he spoke of his divinity alone, which is not of the world. He did this so that, inasmuch as they inclined to believe he is only a man, Christ might draw them to consider his divinity, so that they would believe he is God, willing to overcome their unbelief about his divinity by the opposition of his divinity alone, omitting for the time being the mention of his human lot.

If Christ is only a man, how can he say, "I came forth from God and came" (John 8:42), when it is clear that man was made by God, not proceeding from God? But just as man did not proceed from God, so the Word of God proceeded, of which it is said, "My heart has uttered a good word" (Psalm 45:1). Since it is from God, it is rightly also with God; and since it was not uttered idly, it rightly does all things, for all things were made through it, and without it nothing was made (John 1:3). But this Word, through which all things were made, is God, since the one who proceeded is the Word, and God is the one who proceeded from God.

If Christ is only a man, how can he say, "If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death forever" (John 8:51)? Not seeing death forever is nothing other than immortality. And immortality is a companion of divinity, because divinity is immortal, and immortality is the fruit of divinity. But every man is mortal; however, immortality cannot come from what is mortal. Therefore, immortality cannot arise from Christ as a mortal man. But he says, "He who keeps my word will not see death forever" (John 8:51). Therefore, Christ's Word provides immortality, and through immortality it provides divinity. If he cannot bestow immortality on another while being mortal himself, but Christ's Word does bestow and provide immortality, then the one who provides immortality is not only a man, because he provides what, if he were only a man, he could not provide. By providing divinity through immortality, he proves himself to be God, offering divinity, which he could not provide if he were not God.

If Christ is only a man, how can he say, "Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58)? For no man can be before Abraham, from whom he himself is; nor can anything be before him from whom he himself originated. But Christ, since he is from Abraham, says that he is before Abraham. Either he is lying and deceiving, if he was not before Abraham, from whom he is; or he is not deceiving, if he is also God, since he was before Abraham. If he had not been, it would follow that, since he is from Abraham, he could not be before Abraham.

If Christ is only a man, how can he say, "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish forever" (John 10:27-28)? But since every man is bound by the laws of mortality and therefore cannot preserve himself forever, much less can he preserve another forever. But Christ promises to give salvation forever; if he does not give it, he is a liar; if he gives it, he is God. But he does not lie; for he gives what he promises. Therefore, he is God, who offers eternal salvation, which a man, who cannot preserve himself, cannot provide to another.

If Christ is only a man, what is the meaning of his saying, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30)? For how can it be said that I and the Father are one, if he is not also God and the Son? Who can be said to be one, because he is from the Father, and because he is the Son of the Father, and because he is born of the Father, and because he is found to have proceeded from the Father; through which he is also God? When the Jews considered this arrogant and blasphemous, because Christ showed himself to be God in these words, and therefore they rushed for stones and prepared to throw them, Christ strongly refuted his adversaries with the example and testimony of the Scriptures. He said, "Is it not written in your Law, 'I said, you are gods'? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, 'You are blaspheming,' because I said, 'I am the Son of God'?" (John 10:34-36, Psalm 82:6). In these words he did not deny that he is God, but rather confirmed that he is God. For since those to whom the word of God came are called gods, much more is this one God, who is found to be better than all of them. And nevertheless, he refuted the calumnious blasphemy with a legitimate argument: for he wants to be understood as God, so that he is the Son of God, and not the Father himself. For he said that he was sent, and he showed that he had performed many works from the Father; from this he wanted to be understood as the Son, not the Father; he made mention of the Son, not the Father, in the last part of his defense. So, as far as the charge of blasphemy is concerned, he says that he is the Son, not the Father; but as far as his divinity is concerned, by saying "I and the Father are one," he proved himself to be the Son and God. Therefore, he is God: but God in such a way that he is the Son, not the Father.
